counterevidence_considered.description: The numerator (26 events) is derived only from the 40 retained sites, so the statistic partly rests on the retained subset; one could argue this smuggles a subset quantity into a complete-domain claim. However, the report discloses exactly this (each removed site contributes 0 confirmed events) and correctly characterizes the result as a lower bound, so the retained-subset value is not being presented as the complete-domain rate — the denominator genuinely covers all 48 planned units.
counterevidence_considered.observed_value: numerator from retained subset, disclosed as contributing 0 per removed site

Prespecified screening rule: a planned nest site is retained only if it received
at least 3 confirmed observation visits during the incubation window. Nest sites
removed by screening have no fledging outcome recorded; each of the 8 removed
nest sites contributes 0 confirmed fledging events to the numerator.

source_refs.quoted_text:
This rate is a complete-planned-set rate: its denominator is all 48 planned nest
sites and its numerator counts only the 26 fledging events confirmed among the 40
retained nest sites. Because the 8 removed nest sites have no recorded outcome,
the reported value is a lower bound on fledging success for the complete planned
set, and no rate for any other denominator is claimed here.

extensions.x-stage1-falsification-attempt: I attempted to establish the issue was present despite appearances. (1) I checked whether the reported 0.5417 could actually be a retained-subset value relabeled as complete-domain: 26/48 = 0.541666..., which half-up rounds to 0.5417, while the retained-subset value would be 26/40 = 0.6500; the reported number matches the planned denominator, and I verified planned=48, retained=40, events=26 directly from inputs/data.csv. (2) I checked the section breakdown for a hidden retained denominator: it uses Fraction(section_events, len(section_rows)), i.e., the planned count per section (e.g., 7/12 = 0.5833), consistent with the complete-domain framing. (3) I considered whether the subset-derived numerator alone constitutes the issue class; it does not, because the report never asserts the retained-subset rate for the complete domain and explicitly labels the result a lower bound with the missing-outcome caveat. I could not falsify the no-issue verdict.
